items.title: SP 800-12 Rev. 1, An Introduction to Information Security
items.creator: NIST
items.why: Section 1.4 defines confidentiality, integrity and availability as three separate properties with three different failure modes, which is exactly the sort the finance-share ticket needs: renamed files break availability, replaced contents break integrity, and reading each file before encrypting it breaks confidentiality. It beats a CIA-triad blog because these are the definitions auditors and incident forms actually cite.
items.struggle: The folder is restored but the ticket still says security incident — which property broke, and which queue owns it?

items.title: Security Engineering: A Guide to Building Dependable Distributed Systems — Chapter 2: Who Is the Opponent?
items.creator: Ross Anderson (University of Cambridge)
items.why: Chapter 2 works through who actually attacks systems — state actors, the cybercrime ecosystem and the specialist markets inside it — and what each one is after, so an agent can ask who benefits from this symptom on a normal call. It beats a hacker-stereotype video because the motive explains the symptom, and the chapter is a free PDF from the author.
items.struggle: How do I ask what an attacker would do next on a support call without accusing the user or probing the host?

items.title: Authentication vs. authorization
items.creator: Microsoft Learn
items.why: Puts the two checks side by side: authentication proves who the caller is, authorization decides what that identity may open. That is the only way to explain a sign-in that succeeds while the finance share still returns Access denied, and it uses the same sign-in and consent vocabulary as the Entra logs the learner will read.
items.struggle: The password worked and the MFA prompt was approved, so how can the user still be denied access to the share?

items.title: Permission denied when accessing VirtualBox shared folder when member of the vboxsf group
items.creator: Super User
items.why: The accepted answer is the lesson: the account was already in the group, a restart changed nothing, and access only worked after logging out and back in, because group membership is read when the session is created. That is the token-age check the lesson asks for, reported by someone who hit it, where a permissions how-to would only tell you how to add the group.
items.struggle: I added the account to the group and even rebooted — why does it still say permission denied?

items.title: Hashing Algorithms and Security - Computerphile
items.creator: Computerphile
items.why: Eight minutes separating a one-way hash from reversible encryption, with collision and password-cracking examples that make the vendor published a SHA-256 so the download is safe claim visibly wrong. A learner who watches this stops treating a matching hash as proof of encryption or of malware-free contents, which is the muddle in the lesson's three-tools section.
items.struggle: The download page lists a SHA-256 value and my hash matches — does that mean the file is encrypted, or that it is safe?

items.title: What does a Let's Encrypt (or other DV) certificate prove?
items.creator: Information Security Stack Exchange
items.why: The answer states it plainly: a DV certificate proves only that whoever requested it controlled the domain at that moment, so a lookalike domain gets the same padlock. That kills the the padlock means the site is legitimate reassurance learners give users, and it beats a TLS explainer because it answers the exact question the lesson's four-things and three-things list is built around.
items.struggle: The phishing site shows a valid green padlock — doesn't the certificate prove the company is real?

items.title: Hacking Websites with SQL Injection - Computerphile
items.creator: Computerphile
items.why: Tom Scott takes a deliberately vulnerable PHP login and shows that the username is pasted straight into the SQL string, so a quote ends the string and the rest of the input is read as SQL — the mechanism behind the lesson's apostrophe-broke-the-order-search ticket. It beats an OWASP category definition because it starts from the string-concatenation mistake instead of a taxonomy.
items.struggle: A customer typed an apostrophe into the order search and got a database error — why does punctuation break the query?

items.title: What is cross-site scripting (XSS) and how to prevent it?
items.creator: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
items.why: The free apprentice labs make the learner put a harmless-looking payload into a search box and watch the page execute it, separating the app stored my text from the app executed my text — the exact gap in the lesson's XSS section. It beats a cheat sheet because the learner reproduces the defect and then sees which output encoding removes it.
items.struggle: The page just prints my name back to me — how is that a security bug if the only person affected is me?

items.title: How can I check from the command line if a reboot is required on RHEL or CentOS?
items.creator: Server Fault
items.why: The top answers give needs-restarting -r with its 0 or 1 exit code, the /var/run/reboot-required flag and the running-versus-installed kernel check, so installed can be turned into effective with a command whose output goes into the ticket. That is the pending-reboot gap the lesson calls out, and it beats a patch-management overview because it is the check itself.
items.struggle: The patch installed and the scanner says compliant — why is the server still running the old kernel?

items.title: Take response actions on a device in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
items.creator: Microsoft Learn
items.why: Shows isolate, contain and restrict app execution as separate remote actions and spells out the proxy case where full isolation can strand a device, which is the difference between containing one laptop and cutting off a site. It beats an EDR explainer because these are the console decisions an L1 will be asked to approve, including when each one is the wrong call.
items.struggle: EDR flagged the laptop but the user is still working — do I isolate it, and what does isolation actually cut off?

items.title: Why are the CVSS scores differ so much between Redhat and NVD page?
items.creator: Information Security Stack Exchange
items.why: The answer puts the two vectors side by side and shows the disagreement sits in human-chosen inputs — attack complexity, scope of impact — not in the arithmetic, so one CVE is 10.0 at NVD and 8.8 at the vendor. That is the lesson's severity-is-the-bug-risk-is-this-host argument with real numbers, and a CVSS calculator cannot settle it.
items.struggle: NVD says 10.0 and the vendor says 8.8 for the same CVE — which number goes on the ticket?

items.title: CVSS v3.1 Specification Document
items.creator: FIRST
items.why: The normative text says the Base score reflects intrinsic severity assuming the reasonable worst case and must be adjusted by Temporal and Environmental metrics for a specific environment, the documented reason a 9.8 on an isolated lab host need not be first on the list. It beats a blog summary because it is what the scanners implement and what an exception register has to argue against.
items.struggle: The scanner says 9.8 critical but the host is an isolated lab box — why isn't this the first thing I patch?
